_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 158 - Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), chs. 18-23: The Two Sorcerers (273-278), The Magical Wooden Head (279-286), Kahukura and the Fairies (287-291), Te Kanawa's Adventure with the Fairies (292-295), The Loves of Takarangi and Rau-mahora (296-300), The Stratagem of Te Ponga's Elopement (301-312). Topics 8 trickster, 5 ritual origin, 9 sacred landscape. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 18, The Two Sorcerers (London 1855)

summary.en: Kiki's shadow withers shrubs; sliding back his door as canoes pass, he kills the crews at a glance - 'the offspring of Kiki wither shrubs'. Tamure of Kawhia crosses the ranges to duel him, repeats the incantation Mata-tawhito before landing, enchants the threshold and door, and feeds his enchanted meal to his daughter, who slips most of it under her clothes. Leaving, Tamure instructs a downstream village to tell pursuers the canoe is far ahead; Kiki's men, misled, turn back, and Kiki dies by Tamure's spells.
summary.zh: 巫師基基的影子能令灌木枯萎；河上舟過，他拉開屋門便使舟中人僵斃——『基基的子嗣使灌木枯萎』。卡菲亞的塔穆雷越山赴會決鬥：登岸前誦『馬塔陶希托』護身咒，到村後詛咒門檻與門扉，又讓女兒吃下詛咒之食——她卻把大部分食物藏於衣下。臨別時他囑下游村人：若有人追問，便答『那舟早已遠去』。基基族人被誤導而折返，基基死於塔穆雷咒術之下。

sensitivity.note: Sorcery-duel legend; Grey notes descendants of both sorcerers were living in his day.

passages.text: Kiki was a celebrated sorcerer and skilled in magical arts; he lived upon the river Waikato. The inhabitants of that river still have this proverb, 'The offspring of Kiki wither shrubs.' This proverb had its origin in the circumstance of Kiki being such a magician that he could not go abroad in the sunshine; for if his shadow fell upon any place not protected from his magic, it at once became tapu, and all the plants there withered. If any parties coming up the river called at his village in their canoes as they paddled by, he still remained quietly at home, but just drew back the sliding door of his house so that it might stand open, and the strangers stiffened and died; or even as canoes came paddling down from the upper parts of the river, he drew back the sliding wooden shutter to the window of his house, and the crews on board were sure to die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 18 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At length the fame of this sorcerer spread exceedingly and resounded through every tribe, until Tamure, a chief who dwelt at Kawhia, thought he would go and contend in the arts of sorcery with Kiki. He selected two of his people as companions and took his young daughter with him; they crossed the mountain range from Kawhia and came down upon the river Waipa, and paddled down towards the village of Kiki, managing so well that before they were seen by anybody they had arrived at the landing-place. Tamure was not only skilled in magic but also a very cautious man; whilst still afloat he repeated an incantation of the kind called Mata-tawhito to preserve him safe from all arts of sorcery, and other incantations to ward off spells, collect good genii round him, keep off evil spirits and shield him from demons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 18 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old sorcerer called out that they were welcome and invited them up; in the square some of Kiki's people kindled fire in an enchanted oven and began to cook food for the strangers. Tamure sat on the ground just outside the entrance to the house and repeated incantations over the threshold, so that Kiki might be enchanted as he stepped over it to come out. When the food was cooked and spread upon clean mats, the old sorcerer made his appearance and invited Tamure to eat with him - but the food was all enchanted, and his object in asking Tamure was that the enchanted food might kill him. Tamure said his young daughter was very hungry and would eat of the food; he kept repeating Mata-tawhito, Whakangungu and Parepare, protections against enchanted food, and as she ate she also continued to repeat them; even when she stretched out her hand to take a sweet potato she dropped the greater part of it at her feet and hid it under her clothes, then only ate a little bit. Kiki waited for Tamure to begin to eat that he might soon die; meanwhile Tamure repeated incantations which might render the door enchanted also, so that Kiki might be certain not to escape when he passed out of it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 18 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tamure now ordered his people to launch his canoe, and they paddled away; a little time after they had left the village Kiki became unwell. As they passed a village where there were many people on the river's bank, Tamure stopped and said to them, 'If you should see any canoe pulling after us, and the people in the canoe ask you, Have you seen a canoe pass up the river? would you be good enough to say, Yes, a canoe has passed by here; and then if they ask you, How far has it got? would you be good enough to say, Oh, by this time it has got very far up the river.' Some time after Tamure's party had left, the old sorcerer became very ill indeed; his people knew this had been brought about by the magical arts of Tamure and sprang into a canoe to follow after him as hard as they could. When they reached the village on the river's bank they called out and asked how far the canoe had reached, and the villagers answered, 'Oh, that canoe must have got very far up the river by this time.' The pursuers, upon hearing this, returned again to their own village, and Kiki died from the incantations of Tamure. He overcame every other sorcerer until he met Tamure, but he was vanquished by him and had to bend the knee before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 18 (1855); not verbatim.

region.en: Sacred Mount fortress near Waitara, Taranaki (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 塔拉納基懷塔拉附近聖山要塞（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 19, The Magical Wooden Head (London 1855)

summary.en: Puarata and Tautohito keep a carved wooden head on the Sacred Mount whose mighty cry kills every traveller who passes; armies sent to destroy the sorcerers all perish, the corpses strewing the track over Waimatuku. Hakawau dreams his genius stands head in heaven and feet on earth, then walks the fatal road in safety, warding off malignant spirits with ceaseless incantations. His genii feign retreat, lead the fortress spirits into pursuit, and storm the undefended place; the wooden head can only wail, and as Hakawau smites the threshold in leaving, every soul in the fortress dies.
summary.zh: 普阿拉塔與陶托希托供奉一尊木雕頭顱於聖山之上：其大吼一聲，過路人便皆斃命；征討的大軍無一生還，屍骸遍布懷馬圖庫道上。大巫哈卡瓦烏夢見自己的精靈頭頂天、腳立地，遂踏上死路卻平安無事。其精靈佯敗誘敵、後軍突襲空城；木雕頭顱只餘低泣。哈卡瓦烏臨行以手拍擊門檻——剛出要塞，全寨之人盡數倒斃。

sensitivity.note: Magic-duel legend; the head's killing cry is the central motif.

passages.text: This head bewitched all persons who approached the hill where the fortress in which it was kept was situated, so that, from fear of it, no human being dared to approach the place, which was thence named the Sacred Mount. Upon that mount dwelt Puarata and Tautohito with their carved head, and its fame went through all the country - to the river Taranaki, to Kaipara, to the tribes of Ngapuhi, to Akau, to Waikato, to Kawhia, to Mokau, to Hauraki, and to Tauranga. Everywhere reports were heard that so great were its magical powers none could escape alive from them; and although many warriors and armies went to the Sacred Mount to try to destroy the sorcerers to whom the head belonged, and to carry it off as a genius for their own district, they all perished in the attempt. No mortal could approach the fortress and live; even parties of people who were travelling along the forest track northwards towards Muriiwhenua all died by the magical powers of that head, whether they went in large armed bodies or simply as quiet travellers - their fate was alike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 19 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the report reached a very powerful sorcerer named Hakawau, who, confiding in his magical arts, said he was resolved to go and see this magic head and the sorcerers who owned it. He called upon all the genii who were subservient to him, in order that he might be thrown into an enchanted sleep and see what his fate in this undertaking would be; and in his slumber he saw that his genius would triumph in the encounter, for it was so lofty and mighty that in his dream its head reached the heavens whilst its feet remained upon earth. Having by his spells ascertained this, he started on his journey with one friend, passing Maraetai, Putataka, Rukuwai, Waitara, Te Weta, and at length reaching the most fatal place of all - Waimatuku. Here they smelt the stench of the carcases of the numbers who had been previously destroyed, so bad that it was quite suffocating; but Hakawau kept on unceasingly working at his enchantments which might ward off the attacks of evil genii and collect good genii about them, and thus they passed over Waimatuku, looking with horror at the many corpses strewed about the beach and in the dense fern and bushes which bordered the path.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 19 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Nevertheless they died not on the dreadful road, but went straight along the path till they came to the place where it passes over some low hills, from whence they could see the fortress which stood upon the Sacred Mount. Hakawau, with his incantations, sent forth many genii to attack the spirits who kept watch over the fortress and magic head; some in advance, charged others to follow at some distance. As soon as the spirits who guarded the fortress saw them, they all issued out to attack; the good genii feigned a retreat, the evil ones following, and whilst they were thus engaged in the pursuit, some of the thousands of good genii stormed the fortress now left without defenders; and when the evil spirits turned to protect the fortress, the genii of Hakawau caught them one after the other, and thus all the spirits of the old sorcerer Puarata were utterly destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 19 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the watchmen of the fortress, to their great surprise, saw strangers coming, Puarata hurried to his magic head to call upon it: 'Strangers, come here! Two strangers come!' But it uttered only a low wailing sound; for since the good genii of Hakawau had destroyed the spirits who served Puarata, the old sorcerer addressed in vain his supplications to the magic head - it could no longer raise aloud its powerful voice as in former times. Could it have cried out with a loud voice, straightway Hakawau and his friend would both have perished; for thus it was, when armies and travellers had in other times passed the fortress, Puarata addressed supplications to his magic head, and when it cried out with a mighty voice, the strangers all perished as they heard it. Hakawau went quietly on over the gateway without paying the least attention to the angry words of those who called out to him, and went direct to all the most holy places of the fortress where no person who had not been made sacred might enter. When at length they departed, he smote his hands on the threshold of the house in which they had rested, and they had hardly got well outside the fortress before every soul in it was dead - not a single one of them was left alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 19 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Kahukura Learns Netting from the Fairies
title.zh: 卡胡庫拉向精靈學織網

region.en: Rangiaowhia beach, far north Aotearoa (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 紐西蘭最北蘭吉奧希亞海灘（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 20, Kahukura and the Fairies (London 1855)

summary.en: Travelling north, Kahukura finds mackerel cleaned on the sand by night footprints and no crushed reeds - fairies fish here. He returns after dark, mixes with the pale-skinned Patupaiarehe hauling their net, and keeps delaying dawn by untying the slip-knot a fairy kindly ties for him, so that his string of fish keeps falling. At full daylight the fairies see he is a man and scatter, abandoning their rush net and flax-stem canoes - and with the net the art of net-making passes to Kahukura, who teaches it to his children and so to the whole Maori race.
summary.zh: 卡胡庫拉北上途中發現沙灘上有人夜間清理鯖魚——足跡卻無蘆草壓痕，必是精靈所為。當夜他潛入精靈的拖網隊伍，因其膚色近乎精靈之白而未被識破；他屢次解開精靈好心替他繫好的結，讓魚串墜地，拖延到天光大亮。精靈們看清他是凡人，倉皇四散，棄網棄舟——舟竟是亞麻莖所化。編網之術從此傳於卡胡庫拉，再由他傳子孫，澤被整個毛利民族。

sensitivity.note: Etiological origin of Maori net-making (Patupaiarehe fairies); interpretive tagging.

passages.text: Once upon a time a man of the name of Kahukura wished to pay a visit to Rangiaowhia, a place lying far to the northward, near the country of the tribe called Te Rarawa. As he was on his road he passed a place where some people had been cleaning mackerel, and he saw the inside of the fish lying all about the sand on the sea-shore; surprised at this, he looked about at the marks, and saw that the people who had been fishing had made their footmarks in the night-time, not that morning, nor in the day. He said to himself, 'These are no mortals who have been fishing here - spirits must have done this; had they been men, some of the reeds and grass which they sat on in their canoe would have been lying about.' He felt quite sure from several circumstances that spirits or fairies had been there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 20 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: That night he returned to the place where he had observed all these things, and just as he reached the spot, back had come the fairies too, to haul their net for mackerel; some of them were shouting out, 'The net here! the net here!' Then a canoe paddled off to fetch the other in which the net was laid, and as they dropped the net into the water they began to cry out, 'Drop the net in the sea at Rangiaowhia, and haul it at Mamaku.' These words were sung out by the fairies as an encouragement in their work and from the joy of their hearts at their sport in fishing. As the fairies were dragging the net to the shore, Kahukura managed to mix amongst them and hauled away at the rope; he happened to be a very fair man, so that his skin was almost as white as that of these fairies, and from that cause he was not observed by them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 20 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the net came close in to the shore the fairies began to cheer and shout, 'Go out into the sea some of you, in front of the rocks, lest the nets should be entangled in Tawatawauia a Teweteweuia', for that was the name of a rugged rock standing out from the sandy shore. When the first fish reached the shore, thrown up in the ripples driven before the net, the fairies had not yet remarked Kahukura, for he was almost as fair as they were. It was just at the very first peep of dawn that the fish were all landed; every one took up what fish he liked and ran a twig through their gills, calling out, 'Make haste, run here, all of you, and finish the work before the sun rises.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 20 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kahukura kept on stringing his fish with the rest of them. He had only a very short string, and, making a slip-knot at the end of it, when he had covered the string with fish, he lifted them up, but had hardly raised them from the ground when the slip-knot gave way from the weight of the fish, and off they fell. Then some of the fairies ran good-naturedly to help him to string his fish again, and one of them tied the knot at the end of the string for him; but the fairy had hardly gone after knotting it before Kahukura had unfastened it and again tied a slip-knot at the end. Then he began stringing his fish again, and when he had got a great many on, up he lifted them, and off they slipped as before. This trick he repeated several times, delaying the fairies in their work by getting them to knot his string for him. At last full daylight broke, so that there was light enough to distinguish a man's face, and the fairies saw that Kahukura was a man; then they dispersed in confusion, leaving their fish and their net, and abandoning their canoes, which were nothing but stems of the flax. Now was first discovered the stitch for netting a net, for they left theirs with Kahukura, and it became a pattern for him. He thus taught his children to make nets, and by them the Maori race were made acquainted with that art, which they have now known from very remote times.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 20 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Te Kanawa Offers the Fairies the Shadows of His Jewels
title.zh: 特卡納瓦以珠影贈精靈

region.zh: 紐西蘭懷卡托普凱莫爾山（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 21, Te Kanawa's Adventure with the Fairies (London 1855)

summary.en: Kiwi-hunting overnight on Mount Pukemore, Te Kanawa's party hear a whole troop of fairies - men, women and children - approaching in the dark. They peep over the great tree-roots at the handsome chief whenever the fire burns low, singing merrily. Te Kanawa, nearly frightened to death, hangs his greenstone neck-ornament and ear-rings on a stick as an offering; the fairies take only the shadows of the jewels, handing them from one to another, and vanish - leaving the jewels themselves, 'the hearts of the fairies being quite contented at getting the shadows alone'.
summary.zh: 特卡納瓦一行夜宿普凱莫爾山頂獵奇維鳥，黑暗中忽然聽見大隊精靈——男女老幼——歡歌而來。火光一暗，精靈便從巨樹盤根後偷看這位俊美酋長。特卡納瓦嚇得半死，心生一計：將碧玉頸飾與耳環繫於木棒獻上。精靈們只取寶石的影子，一一傳遞把玩，隨即消失無蹤——寶石原物留了下來，『精靈的心，得影即足』。

sensitivity.note: Fairy-encounter tale; Grey notes the fairies' fair hair and skin, unlike the Maori.

passages.text: Te Kanawa, a chief of Waikato, was the man who fell in with a troop of fairies upon the top of Puke-more, a high hill in the Waikato district. This chief happened one day to go out to catch kiwis with his dogs, and when night came on he found himself right at the top of Puke-more. So his party made a fire to give them light, for it was very dark. They had chosen a tree to sleep under - a very large tree with immense roots sticking up high above the ground; they slept between these roots, and made the fire beyond them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 21 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as it was dark they heard loud voices, like the voices of people coming that way; there were the voices of men, of women, and of children, as if a very large party of people were coming along. They looked for a long time but could see nothing; till at last Te Kanawa knew the noise must proceed from fairies. His people were all dreadfully frightened, and would have run away if they could; but where could they run to? for they were in the midst of a forest, on the top of a lonely mountain, and it was dark night. For a long time the voices grew louder and more distinct as the fairies drew nearer and nearer, until they came quite close to the fire; Te Kanawa and his party were half dead with fright.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 21 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the fairies approached to look at Te Kanawa, who was a very handsome fellow. To do this, they kept peeping slily over the large roots of the tree under which the hunters were lying, and kept constantly looking at him whilst his companions were quite insensible from fear. Whenever the fire blazed up brightly, off went the fairies and hid themselves, peeping out from behind stumps and trees; and when it burnt low, back they came close to it, merrily singing as they moved: 'Here you come climbing over Mount Tirangi to visit the handsome chief of Ngapuhi, whom we have done with.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 21 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: A sudden thought struck Te Kanawa, that he might induce them to go away if he gave them all the jewels he had about him; so he took off a beautiful little figure carved in green jasper which he wore as a neck ornament, and a precious carved jasper ear-drop from his ear. Te Kanawa was only trying to amuse and please them to save his life, but all the time he was nearly frightened to death. He took a stick, and fixing it into the ground, hung his neck ornament and ear-rings upon it. As soon as the fairies had ended their song, they took the shadows of the ear-rings and handed them about from one to the other until they had passed through the whole party, which then suddenly disappeared, and nothing more was seen of them. The fairies carried off with them the shadows of all the jewels of Te Kanawa, but they left behind them his jasper neck ornament and his ear-rings, so that he took them back again, the hearts of the fairies being quite contented at getting the shadows alone; they saw, also, that Te Kanawa was an honest, well-dispositioned fellow. However, the next morning, as soon as it was light, he got down the mountain as fast as he could without stopping to hunt longer for kiwis.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 21 (1855); not verbatim.

title.en: Takarangi Carries Water to the Besieged

region.zh: 紐西蘭塔拉納基瓦卡雷瓦要塞（象徵性定位）

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 22, The Loves of Takarangi and Rau-mahora (London 1855)

summary.en: Investing the fortress of Rangirarunga, the Ngati-Awa army leaves its people dying of thirst. The aged chief cries for one drop of water, and calabashes are broken in his hands by the hard-hearted. Seeing his white heron plume, the old man challenges the young leader: can he still the wrathful surge? 'The wrathful surge shall be stilled; this arm of mine is one which no dog dares to bite.' Takarangi fills a calabash at Fount Oringi in dead silence and carries it up - for himself, he is thinking of Rau-mahora, the daughter. They gaze long at each other, she consents to be his bride, and the war ends for ever.
summary.zh: 納蒂阿瓦大軍圍困瓦卡雷瓦要塞，城中糧水俱絕。老酋長在牆頭哀求一滴水，心狠者當眾打碎水葫蘆。他望見敵酋頭上白鷺羽飾，便高聲發問：『你能否平息這憤怒的浪濤？』塔卡蘭基朗聲答道：『浪濤必平；吾臂非犬可噬。』他自奧林吉泉注滿葫蘆，萬軍肅然；葫蘆遞上牆頭——『這水給你，也給那年輕的姑娘。』兩人久久對視；姑娘應允下嫁，干戈就此永息。

sensitivity.note: Grey names the descendants dwelling in Wellington (Te Puni) as living witness of the genealogy.

passages.text: There was, several generations since, a chief of the Taranaki tribe named Rangirarunga. His pa was called Whakarewa; it was a large pa, renowned for the strength of its fortifications. This chief had a very beautiful daughter whose name was Rau-mahora; she was so celebrated for her beauty that the fame of it had reached all parts of these islands, and had come to the ears of Te Rangi-apitirua, a chief of the Ngati-Awa tribes, whose pa was Puke-ariki, on the hill where the Governor's house stood in New Plymouth. This chief had a son named Takarangi; he was the hero of his tribe, and it may be that his heart sometimes dwelt long on the thoughts of such great loveliness. In those days there arose a war between the tribes of Te Rangi-apitirua and of the father of Rau-mahora.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 22 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The army of the Ngati-Awa tribes marched to Taranaki to attack the pa of Rangirarunga, and the army invested that fortress and sat before it night and day, yet they could not take it; they constantly made assaults, so that its inhabitants became worn out from want of provisions and water, and many of them were near dying. At last the old chief of the pa, Rangirarunga, overcome by thirst, stood on the top of the defences and cried out to the men of the enemy's army, 'I pray you to give me one drop of water.' Some of his enemies, pitying the aged man, said 'Yes', and one ran with a calabash to give him water; but the majority, being more hard-hearted, were angry at this, and broke the calabash in his hands, so that not a drop reached the poor old man; and this was done several times, whilst his enemies continued disputing amongst themselves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 22 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old chief still stood on the top of the earthen wall, and he saw the leader of the hostile force with the symbols of his rank fastened on his head - a long white comb made from the bone of a whale, and a plume of the long downy feathers of the white heron, the emblems of his chieftainship. Then was heard by all the voice of the aged man as he shouted from the top of the wall, 'Who art thou?' And the other cried out, 'Lo, he who stands here before you is Takarangi.' And the aged chief called down to him, 'Young warrior, art thou able to still the wrathful surge which foams on the hidden rocks of the shoal of O-rongo-mai-ta-kupe?' meaning, hast thou, although a chief, power to calm the wrath of these fierce men? Then proudly replied the young chief, 'The wrathful surge shall be stilled; this arm of mine is one which no dog dares to bite' - meaning that no plebeian hand dared touch his arm, made sacred by his deeds and rank, or to dispute his will.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 22 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: But what Takarangi was really thinking in his heart was, 'That dying old man is the father of Rau-mahora, of that so lovely maid. Ah, how I should grieve if one so young and innocent should die tormented with the want of water.' Then he arose, and slowly went to bring water for that aged man and for his youthful daughter; he filled a calabash, dipping it up from the cool spring which gushes up from the earth and is named Fount Oringi. No word was spoken or movement made by the crowd of fierce and angry men, but all, resting upon their arms, looked on in wonder and in silence. Calm lay the sea that was before so troubled, all timid and respectful in the lowly hero's presence; and the water was taken by Takarangi and by him held up to the aged chief. Then was heard by all the voice of Takarangi as he cried aloud to him, 'There - said I not to you, No dog would dare to bite this hand of mine? Behold the water for you - for you and for that young girl.' Then they drank, both of them, and Takarangi gazed eagerly at the young girl, and she too looked eagerly at Takarangi; long time gazed they, each one at the other; and as the warriors of the army looked on, lo, he had climbed up and was sitting at the young maiden's side; and they said amongst themselves, 'O comrades, our lord Takarangi loves war, but one would think he likes Rau-mahora almost as well.' At last a sudden thought struck the heart of the aged chief, so he said to his daughter, 'O my child, would it be pleasing to you to have this young chief for a husband?' and the young girl said, 'I like him.' Then the old man consented that his daughter should be given as a bride to Takarangi, and he took her as his wife. Thence was that war brought to an end, and the army dispersed, each man to his own village, and they came back no more to make war against the tribes of Taranaki - for ever were ended their wars against them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 22 (1855); not verbatim.

title.zh: 普希惠亞私奔芒加懷烏

region.en: Mount Eden fortress, Tamaki isthmus, Aotearoa
region.zh: 紐西蘭伊甸山要塞，塔馬基地峽

source.work: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology and Ancient Traditional History of the New Zealand Race, ch. 23, The Stratagem of Puhihuia's Elopement with Te Ponga (London 1855)

summary.en: After a war of stalemates, Waikato makes peace with the fortress town on Mount Eden. At the welcome dance Puhihuia, daughter of the chief, dances 'her full-orbed eyes clear and brilliant as the full moon', and Te Ponga's heart grows wild. His slave's stratagem: call loudly for water, let the chieftainess fetch it. 'You are the water that I thirsted for', says Te Ponga at the spring; they arrange to escape. At the farewell, Puhihuia slips behind scoria rocks and runs; canoes are pre-cut of lashings and plugs, and the pursuing war party can drag only top-sides off the beach, cursing in vain.
summary.zh: 懷卡托人與伊甸山要塞僵持不下，終於議和。歡迎之夜的舞會上，酋長之女普希惠亞『明眸皎如初升滿月』，令客人首領特蓬加心旌搖蕩。他的奴僕獻計：大聲喊渴，引酋長之女親自取水。泉邊相會，特蓬加道：『你就是我所渴的水。』二人約定私奔。辭別宴上，普希惠亞閃身躲入火山岩後疾奔；早被割斷繫繩拔掉木塞的獨木舟令追兵徒勞無功，只能呆立灘頭。

passages.text: There was formerly a large fortified town upon Mount Eden; its defences were massive and strong, and a great number of persons inhabited the town. In the days of olden time a war was commenced by the tribes of Awhitu and of Waikato against the people who inhabited the town at Mount Eden or Maunga-whau. They engaged in a fierce war: one side first persisted in their efforts for victory until they were successful in beating the other party; then the other side in their turn succeeded in resisting their enemies and gained a victory in their turn; thus the tribes of Waikato did not succeed in destroying their enemies as they desired. Seeing no way to accomplish this, they determined to make peace; so at last they arranged a peace, and it appeared to be a sure one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When this peace had been made, Te Ponga, a chief from Awhitu, and one of the fiercest enemies of the people of that town, went attended by a large company to Maunga-whau; the people ran to the gates of the fortress calling out, 'Welcome, oh welcome, strangers from afar!' The strangers walked direct to the large court-yard in front of the house of the chief of the town, and there they all seated themselves. The chiefs of each party stood up and made speeches; the women lighted fires to cook food for the strangers, and when the ovens were opened the food was ranged in a long pile before the visitors. The strangers, however, ate very slowly, knowing they had better take but little food, in order not to surfeit themselves, and so that their waists might be slim when they stood up in the ranks of the dancers; and as they sat they kept on thinking, 'When will night come and the dance begin?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as it began to get dark the dancers began, and whilst they sprang nimbly about, Puhihuia, the young daughter of the chief of the village, stood watching a good opportunity to bound forward before the assembly; when the beating time by the assembly with their feet and hands and the deep voices of the men were all in exact unison, was the fitting moment for her to bound forward into the dance. Then, just as they were all beating time together, Puhihuia perceived the proper moment had come, and forth she sprang before the assembled dancers; first she bends her head with many gestures towards the people upon the one side, and then towards those upon the other, as she performed her part beautifully; her full-orbed eyes seemed clear and brilliant as the full moon rising in the horizon, and whilst the strangers looked at the young girl they all were quite overpowered with her beauty, and Te Ponga, their young chief, felt his heart grow wild with emotion when he saw so much loveliness before him. Then up sprang the strangers to dance in their turn; the young chief Te Ponga stood peeping over them, and at last forth he bounded, and he, too, performed beautifully! The people of the village were so surprised at his agility and grace that they could do nothing but admire him, and as for the young girl Puhihuia, her heart conceived a warm passion for Te Ponga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: At length the dance concluded, and all dispersed; all reclined in slumber except Te Ponga, who lay tossing from side to side, unable to sleep from his great love for the maiden, and devising scheme after scheme. At last a project originated in the suggestions of his private slave, who said, 'Sir, I have found out a plan by which you may accomplish your wishes. To-morrow evening, just at nightfall, as you sit in the court-yard of the chief of the village, feign to be very thirsty, and call to me to bring you a draught of water; I will take care to be at a distance, but do you continue to shout loudly and angrily to me, Sirrah, I want water, fetch me some - call loudly, so that the father of the young girl may hear; then he will probably say to his daughter, My child, why do you let our guest call in that way for water without running to fetch some for him? Then, when the young girl runs down the hill to fetch water from the fountain for you, do you follow her to the spring; but when you rise to follow her, pretend to be in a great passion with me - Where is that deaf slave of mine? I'll go and find the fellow.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: The next evening Te Ponga called out loudly for water, louder and louder, until the chief of the village said to his young daughter, 'My child, run and fetch some water for our guest; why do you allow him to go on calling for water in that way?' Then the maiden arose, and, taking a calabash, went off to fetch water; and no sooner did Te Ponga see her starting off than he too arose and went out of the house, feigning by his voice to be very angry with his slave, but as soon as he was out he went straight after the young girl, led by her voice, who tripped along the path singing blithely and merrily as she went. When the maiden arrived at the brink of the fountain and was about to dip her calabash into it, she heard some one behind her, and, turning suddenly round - ah! there stood Te Ponga himself. She stood quite astonished for some time, and at length asked, 'What can have brought you here?' He answered, 'I came here for a draught of water.' But the girl replied, 'Ha, indeed! Did not I come here to draw water for you? Why, then, did you come?' Then Te Ponga answered, 'You are the water that I thirsted for.' She thought within herself, 'He, then, has fallen in love with me'; they conversed together, and before they separated they arranged a time when they might escape together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the appointed time had arrived, he desired some chosen men of his followers to go to the landing-place on Manuka harbour, where the canoes were all hauled on shore, there to prepare one canoe in which he and all his followers might escape, to launch it and keep it afloat with every paddle in its place, and further to go round every one of the other canoes, to cut the lashings which made the top sides fast to the hulls, and to pull out all the plugs, so that those following them might find they had no canoes in which to continue the pursuit. The next morning Te Ponga, having told his host that he must return to his own country, was presented with the chief's jade mere to establish the peace, and gave his own jade mere in turn. Just before the strangers started, Puhihuia and some of the young girls of the village stole a little way along the road to accompany the strangers; Puhihuia's father seeing his daughter was going so far called out, 'Children, children, come back here!' The other girls stopped, but Puhihuia's heart beat but to the one thought of escaping with her beloved Te Ponga. So she began to run. She drew near to some large scoria rocks and glided behind them, and, when hidden from the view of those in the village, she redoubled her speed - well done, well done, young girl! She runs so fast that her body bends low as she speeds forward. When Te Ponga saw Puhihuia running in this hurried manner, he called aloud to his men, 'What is the meaning of this? let us be off as fast as we can too.' Then began a swift flight, like a feather drifting before the gale. When the people of the village saw that their young chieftainess was gone, there was a wild rushing to and fro for weapons, and whilst they thus lost their time the elopement went unmolestedly on its way. When the pursuers came out ready for the pursuit and laid hold of another canoe to haul it down towards the water, the lashings of the top sides were cut - they dragged nothing but the top sides, there lay the bottom of the canoe unmoved. Pursuit was impossible; the party that had come to make peace escaped, and returned uninjured and joyful to their own country, carrying off with them the young chieftainess, who could only be seen standing on the shore stamping with rage and threatening them in vain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of George Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 23 (1855); not verbatim.
